new_statements.rule_in_words: The book is a comparative segmental phonology (sound inventory, Proto-Ful, dialect sound changes) with no section on accent or tone. Word stress enters only incidentally: Klingenheben reports Westermann's transcription convention for the Ful of the Hausa states, under which main stress ('Starkton') on the penultimate syllable is the unmarked default and a stress mark is written only when some other syllable is stressed; and in a footnote he himself invokes 'the penultimate accent' as the force that lengthened an epenthetic vowel in the Fouta-Sénégalais (Pulaar) form wapańēɓe from Gaden. So the work presupposes a penultimate word accent in Ful as the normal case, with lexically marked departures (Westermann's marked forms), without analysing it.
new_statements.exceptions: Implicit only: Westermann's Handbuch marks the words whose stress is not penultimate (no list or rule given here). § 108 n. 2 (p. 140) merely lists 'Akzent (im weitesten Sinne)' among possible conditioning factors of sound change.
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Ful as a whole: Part I is explicitly 'Der Lautbestand des Ful der Hausastaaten' (Sokoto/Adamawa, i.e. Nigerian Fulfulde, after Westermann 1909/1913), Parts II-IV draw on Futa Jallon (Reichardt, Arensdorff), Fouta Sénégalais = Pulaar (Gaden 1913-14 'Poular I/II'), Masina, Adamaua, Bagirmi sources. The p. 22 stress remark is about Westermann's Hausa-states Ful; the p. 58 'Pänultima-Akzent' remark is applied to a Pulaar (Fouta Sénégalais) form from Gaden.

tone_statements.quote: Fula is a non-tonal Atlantic language spoken across the West African Sahel from Mauritania and Senegal in the west to Sudan and Central African Republic in the east. There is significant dialectal diversity among Fula speakers, and although the morphological, syntactic, and phonological basis of the language is more or less consistent across dialects, many details are quite different. In particular, accounts of syllable prominence suggest that there are striking prosodic differences between dialects.
tone_statements.summary: States Fula is non-tonal; no lexical tone. Praat measures of Senegalese Fuutankoore Pulaar find no pitch difference between syllables; word stress is initial, cued by intensity, weight-insensitive.

sources.quote: 7. Accent. The accent is predominantly a stress accent, and, generally speaking, depends on the long vowels. For disyllables the rules are: (1) If the first vowel is long or diphthongal it has the accent, ex. [sudu, house; ... cows; ... riches]. (2) If the word has two consonants in the middle, or the first vowel is short, the accent is even, ex. nagge, cow. ... horse. (3) In the following cases the accent is on the last syllable: (a) The negative of the past tense; ex. o warai, he did not come. ... (b) nogas, twenty. In trisyllables the rules are: (1) If the penultimate vowel is long it has the accent, ex. lamido, a chief. rawandu, dog. (2) If the penultimate vowel is short the accent is on the first vowel, whether it is long or short, ex. ... the shea tree; but ... shea trees. derewol, paper. ... he was content. All trisyllabic derived verbs follow [hemti]. In polysyllables the accent is free, but is usually on the penultimate, unless a long vowel attracts it to another syllable

tone.quote: Fula is a non-tonal Atlantic language spoken across the West African Sahel from Mauritania and Senegal in the west to Sudan and Central African Republic in the east. There is significant dialectal diversity among Fula speakers, and although the morphological, syntactic, and phonological basis of the language is more or less consistent across dialects, many details are quite different. In particular, accounts of syllable prominence suggest that there are striking prosodic differences between dialects.
